title: The seed of the banyan
hookLine: a father has his son break open a banyan seed and find nothing, and the whole year comes down to one line
carry: tat tvam asi: that you are
tomorrow: why does the greatest war story start with snakes?
last: THE SELF IS KNOWN, NOT EARNED.

lines: BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.
cards: A son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, isn't so sure. He points at a great banyan tree.
Bring me one of its fruits. Here it is, sir. Break it.
It's broken, sir. What do you see? Tiny seeds.
Break one of those. Done. What do you see now?

teach.h: AN ESSENCE TOO FINE TO SEE.
teach.b: This is the Chandogya Upanishad, where year two began.

teach.h: THE WHOLE BANYAN STANDS ON IT.
teach.b: Uddalaka says: that fine essence you can't see, my son, out of it this whole great banyan stands. That finest essence is the Self of all that is. That is the real.
And you are that, Shvetaketu. Tat tvam asi.
It's counted among the great sayings of the Upanishads, the mahavakyas, and here's the teaching plainly: the deepest Self in you, atman, and Brahman, the reality behind everything, are not strangers.
What you can't see holds up what you can. That line sits under this whole year.

You heard Uddalaka again with salt dissolved in water: you can't see it, but every sip tastes of it. You heard Gargi pressing her questions. You read Patanjali defining yoga as the stilling of the turnings of the mind.
You walked Valmiki's whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You kept a year of festivals.
And this week, three paths: karma, bhakti, and jnana.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.
teach.b: Hindus don't all hear tat tvam asi the same way. Shankara's school hears it as one reality: you are Brahman. Ramanuja's hears the Lord living within you as your inner Self, inseparable from you, while you stay you.
Both keep returning to this root. Year two was the root, and later teachers, and poets like Kamban and Tulsidas who retold Valmiki, keep coming back to it.
Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a fire built for snakes.

how: Hindus often mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.

o: a summit: the highest point of a long climb
a seed: a new beginning planted for next year
root: the source texts later teachers return to

games.q: year two in four blocks — tap the pairs.
p: tat tvam asi, that you are
yoga stills the turnings of the mind

s: tat tvam asi basically means 'be yourself'
it says the unseen essence of everything, the Self, is what you are: atman and Brahman are not strangers.
Shvetaketu found nothing inside the banyan seed
and out of that unseen essence, his father said, the whole great tree stands: that you are.
all Hindu schools read these texts the same way
they share the roots but read them differently, as Shankara's and Ramanuja's traditions do.

games.q: Uddalaka has his son break a banyan seed, and he finds nothing inside. what's the father's point?
o: the unseen essence that grows the tree is the Self of all, and that you are.
small things grow big if you work hard enough.
the seed was empty, so the tree isn't really there.
games.why: Chandogya 6.12: out of that fine essence the great banyan stands; it is the Self; tat tvam asi, that you are, Shvetaketu.

practice: If there's a seed nearby, a peppercorn, a mustard seed, a grain of rice, hold it in your palm. Somewhere in it, Uddalaka would say, is a whole plant you can't see.
Then let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, the stilling of the mind, missing God is love, you are the tenth. Hold it on the breath, in on the first half, out on the second.

wordCard.voice: Mula. The root. The banyan stands on what you can't see, and later Hindu teachers keep returning to these roots: the Upanishads, Patanjali, Valmiki.

orig.note: Sanskrit mūla, root: the texts of year two are the roots later Hindu teachers keep returning to.

carryVoice: Keep this: tat tvam asi, that you are. The branches come next. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.
